text.tspan: Public Opinion Compared to General Persuasive
Messaging, and What Are the Implications
The emergence of large language models (LLMs) as tools for automated political messaging
represents a qualitative shift in the landscape of computational persuasion. This paper
compares the mechanisms and effects of LLM-driven political microtargeting against earlier
algorithmic influence systems, drawing on Cathy O'Neil's Weapons of Math Destruction and
the 2024 experimental study by Hackenburg and Margetts. While GPT-4-generated messages
can shift political opinions, microtargeted messaging does not consistently outperform
generic messaging. The paper argues that the more significant finding is the structural
harm LLMs introduce at scale: expanded reach, compounded opacity, and amplified
demographic exploitation, raising new concerns for the integrity of democratic discourse.

g.text: Keywords: large language models, political microtargeting, democratic fairness,
computational persuasion, algorithmic opacity, digital democracy
